title: Confirmation Bias (Everyday Form)
description: We seek, interpret, and remember information that fits our pre-existing beliefs, and ignore or dismiss contrary evidence.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We seek, interpret, and remember information that fits our pre-existing beliefs, and ignore or dismiss contrary evidence.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: Reading news that aligns with your political leaning and feeling it’s “accurate,” while instantly spotting bias in opposing outlets.
A manager who believes an employee is lazy notices every time the employee takes a break, but overlooks the extra hours they stayed late.
After a first date, you remember only the moments that confirm your initial impression, whether positive or negative.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Asking leading questions (“You didn’t like that, did you?”).
Stopping research as soon as you find something that agrees with you.
Sharing articles based on headlines that match your view without reading them fully.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “That source is biased” (only applied to opposing sources).

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You feel a flash of annoyance when someone presents a counter-argument.
You can’t explain the other side’s strongest argument.
Your social circle is homogeneous and reinforces shared views.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: It reduces cognitive effort and protects ego. The brain prefers validation over accuracy. Wason (1960) demonstrated it experimentally with the 2-4-6 task: participants sought only confirmatory examples.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Actively seek disconfirming evidence: “What would prove me wrong?”
Play devil’s advocate with yourself for two minutes before deciding.
Consume media from sources you usually distrust, purely to understand their reasoning.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking this is a problem for “other people.”
Over-correcting into false equivalence (giving equal weight to all sides when evidence is overwhelmingly on one side).

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A hiring manager believes remote employees are less productive. She scrutinizes one remote worker’s deliverables, finding every minor delay, while ignoring the same delays from in-office staff. Her belief solidifies, and she eventually argues against remote work based on her “observations.”

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: What you look for is what you’ll find. Change the question, not just the search.
